answers.summary: Agency small-loan money is pricing roughly 6.4% to 7.1% on a 10-year fixed as of late October 2026, depending on leverage. That's about 1.5 to 2.2 points over a 10-year Treasury sitting near 5%. Fannie Small covers $1M to $9M. In April 2026 Freddie replaced its SBL program with Conventional Small, which runs $2M to $10M.
answers.answer:
### Where rates are
Greystone's August 11, 2026 sheet priced **Fannie Mae Small** 10-year fixed loans at spreads of **176–216 bps** at 80% LTV/1.25x, **156–196** at 65%/1.35x and **146–176** at 55%/1.55x. The 10-year Treasury was 4.69% that day. It then climbed to about 5.1–5.2% in mid-October and was **4.96% on Oct. 22, 2026**. The same spreads on today's index work out to roughly:

| Leverage tier | 10-yr fixed, est. late Oct 2026 |
|---|---|
| 80% / 1.25x | ~6.7%–7.1% |
| 65% / 1.35x | ~6.5%–6.9% |
| 55% / 1.55x | ~6.4%–6.7% |

Freddie small pricing on the same August sheet was similar: **6.40%–7.05%** for a 10-year fixed at 80%. These are estimates. Spreads move weekly, so get a live quote.

### Program terms
| | Fannie Mae Small | Freddie Optigo Conventional Small |
|---|---|---|
| Loan size | $1M–$9M | Generally $2M–$10M |
| Property | 5+ units | 5–50 units, mostly market-rate |
| Terms | 5–30 yr fixed | 5, 7, 10, 12, 15 yr |
| Amortization | 30 yr | 30 yr max |
| Max LTV / min DSCR | 80% (75% cash-out) / 1.25x | tiers; ~80%/1.25x top tier |
| Prepay | Yield maintenance or step-down | YM, then 2-yr lockout, then defeasance; step-down costs extra |
| Recourse | Non-recourse w/ carve-outs | Non-recourse w/ carve-outs |

Freddie's **Conventional Small replaced the Small Balance Loan (SBL) program on April 15, 2026**. Liquidity is not the problem: FHFA set 2026 caps at **$88B per agency**, and workforce-housing loans don't count against them.

### So what
Price is driven by size. Fannie's larger *conventional* loans priced about 50 bps tighter on spread than Small loans (10-yr spread 112–142 at 80% on Sept. 1). For most Ventura County 5–40 unit deals, the binding limit is DSCR, not LTV (see Q108).

Freddie replaced SBL with Optigo Conventional Small on 4/15/2026: generally $2M–$10M, 5–50 units
Aug 11, 2026 Fannie Small 10-yr spread: 176–216 bps at 80%/1.25x over the 10-yr Treasury
10-yr Treasury: 4.69% (Aug 11) to ~4.96% (Oct 22, 2026); implied 10-yr agency small rate ~6.4%–7.1%
FHFA 2026 caps: $88B per agency, workforce housing excluded

The confirmed names are American Riviera Bank, which opened a Ventura lending center in January 2026 and has a 5+ unit multifamily book, and Mechanics Bank, which runs a California multifamily lending group. answers.answer:
### Who is confirmed active
- **American Riviera Bank** (Santa Barbara-based). Opened a **Ventura Lending Center at 1280 S. Victoria Ave.** in January 2026, focused on CRE, construction and real estate investors. It later bought the adjacent 1220 S. Victoria property for a full-service branch. Call-report data shows **$89.5M of 5+ unit multifamily loans, 8.2% of its loan book**, as of 3/31/2026. That figure is bank-wide.
- **Mechanics Bank** (Walnut Creek). Lists multifamily lending and has expanded its multifamily lending team. In December 2025 it agreed to **sell its Fannie Mae DUS business to Fifth Third**, so for agency execution ask Fifth Third. Mechanics itself now lends from its own balance sheet.
- **Chase** runs a dedicated multifamily lending program and is a long-standing small-apartment lender in California.
- **Community West Bank** has Ventura County branches and merged with Central Valley Community Bank in April 2024. I found no confirmation of its current multifamily appetite. Call before putting it on a list.
- **Montecito Bank & Trust**: no evidence found of Ventura County multifamily lending.

### Typical bank terms (verify per lender)
Industry sources describe 2026 banks as **selective and relationship-driven**. They compete hard when the sponsor brings deposits. Compared with agency loans, bank loans usually mean:
- **Recourse** (full or partial) and a **larger down payment**
- Hybrid fixed periods (often 5–10 years) on 25–30 year amortization
- Lighter third-party reports, faster close, and more flexible prepayment, often step-downs
- Pricing at or slightly above agency, with relationship discounts

### So what
For a $1M–$3M loan, a local bank or credit union often beats the agencies on cost and speed. Fannie Small starts at $1M, and Freddie's floor is $2M. Keep a short list of lenders you've closed with. Banks change their appetite every quarter.

answers.summary: CU SoCal is the clearest confirmed credit union lender. It finances multifamily apartment buildings across Southern California, with up to 30-year amortization and interest-only options. Logix FCU also lists multifamily. Watch the geography, though: Orange County's CU, for example, only lends in OC, LA, Riverside and San Bernardino counties.
answers.answer:
### Confirmed active
- **CU SoCal (Credit Union of Southern California).** Its investment-property page lists **multifamily apartment buildings**, 2–4 unit properties, mixed-use and other CRE in Southern California. Terms: **up to 30-year amortization, up to 15-year term**, interest-only on multifamily, no points, funding in as little as **45 days**. Its posted rates (effective 10/27/2026) were **5/1 ARM 4.85% APR, 7/1 ARM 4.99%, 10-year fixed 5.125%**. Those sit below where agency debt prices, so expect relationship, leverage or credit conditions. Confirm before you quote them.
- **Logix FCU** (Burbank area). Its CRE program lists **multifamily** among eligible property types and advertises up to **70% financing** on investment CRE. 1–4 unit investor loans run through its mortgage side.

### Check geography first
**Orange County's Credit Union** runs a defined 5+ unit program: **$500K–$7.5M, 1.20–1.25x DSCR, 680 FICO, full recourse, no prepayment penalty**. It is **limited to Orange, LA, Riverside and San Bernardino counties**, so it doesn't reach Ventura. Many CUs work this way, which is why you should always ask "do you lend in Ventura County?"

**Ventura County Credit Union** is a licensed local CU (Ventura). I found no published 5+ unit multifamily program, so call before listing it.

### How CU loans differ
- Usually **portfolio loans**: recourse, shorter fixed periods, and often light or no prepayment penalties
- Business lending is limited by regulatory caps, so large loans may be shared as participations
- Fast, simple execution for $500K–$5M loans. That makes CUs a good fit for 5–20 unit Ventura buildings and for 2–4 unit blanket loans

### So what
For a seller with a small building and a buyer who wants flexibility, such as no prepay penalty or interest-only, a CU quote is worth getting next to the Fannie Small quote.

answers.summary: On paper the agencies go to 80% LTV at 1.25x DSCR. In Ventura County, cap rates sit below loan rates, so DSCR limits the loan first and most buyers end up at roughly 50% to 60% LTV. Banks and credit unions typically want 1.20x to 1.25x and 60% to 70% leverage.
answers.answer:
### Headline limits (2026)
| Lender type | Max LTV | Min DSCR |
|---|---|---|
| Fannie Small | 80% (75% cash-out) | 1.25x |
| Freddie Conventional Small | tiered (80%/1.25x top tier on lender grids) | 1.25x+ |
| Freddie Conventional (large) | 65%/1.25x, 60%/1.30x, 55%/1.35x tiers | |
| Banks / CUs | ~60%–75% | 1.20x–1.25x (e.g., OCCU) |
| DSCR loans (1–4 units) | ~70%–75% | ~1.0x; 1.20x+ prices better |

Lender grids also price by tier. On Greystone's August 2026 small sheet, dropping from **80%/1.25x to 55%/1.55x** cut the rate by about **30 bps**.

### Why DSCR limits the loan before LTV
Max LTV under a DSCR test = cap rate ÷ (DSCR × loan constant).

At a **5.25% cap**, **6.75% rate** and 30-year amortization (loan constant **7.78%**), a 1.25x test gives:

5.25 ÷ (1.25 × 7.78) = **about 54% LTV**

So the "80% loan" turns into a 54% loan. The buyer brings about 46% equity, or negotiates price. Interest-only periods and lower-leverage pricing tiers help a little.

Lenders also use **their own underwritten NOI**, not the broker's pro forma: in-place rents (Q109), a vacancy factor, actual insurance quotes (Q111), and replacement reserves. Underwritten NOI is often several percent below the seller's number.

### So what
- Ask for a lender sizing early. Make the OM's NOI match how a lender will underwrite it.
- Buyers needing high leverage (1031 replacement debt, thin equity) may need a bank with recourse, seller carry (Q113) or mezzanine debt.
- A cap rate below the loan rate is **negative leverage**: each dollar of debt lowers the cash-on-cash return.
keyPoints: Agency small: 80% max LTV (75% cash-out), 1.25x min DSCR
Max LTV under DSCR = cap rate ÷ (DSCR × loan constant)
5.25% cap, 6.75% rate, 30-yr amortization (7.78% constant), 1.25x: about 54% LTV
Lenders size on underwritten in-place NOI with vacancy, actual insurance and reserves
Banks/CUs commonly 1.20x–1.25x DSCR

answers.summary: Nearly every lender will finance buildings with below-market or restricted rents, but they size the loan on in-place rents, not on rents you hope to reach. For deed-restricted or affordable properties, agency affordable programs and FHA often give the best terms, and some reach 90% LTV on LIHTC deals.
answers.answer:
### The core rule
Lenders **underwrite current in-place rental income**, with no trending or credit for future rent bumps. That matters a lot in Ventura County:
- **AB 1482** caps most covered units at 5% + CPI, max 10% a year.
- **Oxnard's rent stabilization ordinance** (adopted 2022) caps many annual increases at **4%** and **sunsets 12/31/2030**.
- Long-term tenants in older buildings are often 20%–40% under market.

So a building with low in-place rents gets a smaller loan, whatever the upside.

### Who to call, by situation
| Situation | Best fit |
|---|---|
| Stabilized, rents under market, no recorded restrictions | Fannie Small / Freddie Conventional Small, banks, CUs, all sized on in-place NOI |
| Value-add, heavy turnover planned | Bank or CU (recourse) or debt-fund bridge; sized on in-place, with the business plan judged on how fast rents can legally reset |
| Recorded affordability (LIHTC, regulatory agreement) | Fannie/Freddie affordable and preservation executions, FHA 223(f) |
| Section 8 HAP contract | Fannie or FHA. *Freddie Conventional Small lists HAP contracts as ineligible* |

### Affordable pricing (Greystone, Aug 11, 2026; loans over $6M–$10M)
- Fannie **Preservation** 10-yr: about **6.03%**, 80% LTV, **1.20x**
- Fannie/Freddie **9% LIHTC**: about 6.3%–6.5%, up to **90% LTV, 1.15x**, up to 40-yr amortization
- **FHA 223(f)**: 5.75%–6.22% net of MIP (over $7.5M)

The agencies have a policy reason to like these deals. FHFA requires **at least 50%** of agency multifamily volume to be mission-driven, and **workforce-housing loans are excluded from the 2026 caps**.

### So what
For a seller with a rent-controlled building, the buyer's loan, and so the price, depends on **current rents**. Show a rent roll that makes clear which units are at market and how fast units turn over. For restricted or affordable assets, steer buyers to an affordable specialist, not a generalist bank.
keyPoints: Lenders size on in-place rents, not projected rent increases
Oxnard RSO caps many increases at 4% and sunsets 12/31/2030; AB 1482 caps at 5% + CPI (max 10%)
Fannie Preservation 10-yr was about 6.03% at 80%/1.20x (Aug 2026); 9% LIHTC up to 90% LTV/1.15x
Freddie Conventional Small treats HAP contracts as ineligible
FHFA: at least 50% of agency volume must be mission-driven; workforce housing excluded from 2026 caps

answers.summary: Both are active in California multifamily, but they rarely play in Ventura County's typical small-building deal. Life companies want large, stabilized, low-leverage assets. Debt funds, with 275+ platforms in 2026, fill the transitional and value-add niche at higher cost.
answers.answer:
### Life insurance companies
- In 2026 they are **highly selective but active**, with allocations aimed at **high-quality, stabilized multifamily**, durable cash flow and **conservative leverage**.
- Some are shifting toward **shorter-duration** loans to match their annuity business.
- California example: in **July 2026** Slatt Capital placed a life-company loan with **PPM America** on a Novato apartment refinance: **10-year term, 30-year amortization**.
- **Ventura County fit**: the newer, larger, institutional apartment communities in Thousand Oaks, Camarillo, Oxnard, Simi Valley and Ventura that trade to institutions. They are rarely a fit for a 1960s 12-unit building.

### Debt funds and bridge lenders
- Over **275 active platforms**. They are the main source of **transitional** money: lease-ups, value-add, recapitalizations and loans bought from other lenders.
- They underwrite **downside protection and basis**, not aggressive rent growth. Floating rates and higher spreads than agency are typical.
- **Bridge-to-bridge** refinancing is now common.
- **Ventura County fit**: value-add repositions, buildings with high vacancy or deferred maintenance that agencies won't take yet, and short-fuse deals such as a 1031 buyer who must close fast.

### Others in the mix
- **CMBS** issuance rose 21% in 2025 to **$125.6B**. Good for stabilized, older-vintage assets, but underwriting is rigid and prepayment is inflexible.
- **Banks** and **agencies** still carry most small multifamily volume (Q105–Q107).

### So what
For a typical **5–50 unit** Ventura County listing, plan on agency, bank or CU financing. Bring in a debt-fund quote when the buyer's plan needs speed or a renovation budget. Bring in life-company money for larger, newer, low-leverage deals, where it can offer the lowest rate.
keyPoints: Life companies: selective, stabilized assets, conservative leverage; example 10-yr/30-yr amortization loan in Novato (July 2026)
Debt funds: 275+ platforms; the main source of transitional and value-add capital
CMBS issuance rose 21% in 2025 to $125.6B
Typical Ventura County 5–50 unit deals go agency, bank or CU, not life company

answers.summary: Lenders still lend in fire zones, but the loan is sized on the actual insurance premium, so a premium spike cuts DSCR and loan proceeds. They need coverage that meets their replacement-cost and carrier standards, often a California FAIR Plan fire policy plus a DIC wrap. Insurance quotes have become a gating item in due diligence.
answers.answer:
### What lenders require
- **Hazard coverage at replacement cost** (or at least the loan amount) from acceptable carriers, plus the lender's limits on deductibles.
- When standard carriers decline, the common fix is a **California FAIR Plan fire-only policy plus a Difference-in-Conditions (DIC) wrap** for the other perils. Lenders generally accept this if the FAIR Plan limit meets their replacement-cost or loan-amount test. Some lenders have stricter overlays for extreme-risk properties.
- Agency multifamily loans follow detailed insurance chapters in the Fannie and Freddie guides. Check them for deductibles and seismic rules on specific deals.

### How insurance hits underwriting
Insurance is an operating expense, so **every premium dollar comes off NOI and loan proceeds**.
- One broker-newsletter example (not a lender policy): premiums went from **$1,900 to $4,900** and **DSCR fell from 1.17 to 1.06**.
- Some lenders **stress premiums by about +20%**.
- The FAIR Plan has grown fast: residential policies up **151% since Sept 2022**, exposure up **234% to about $700B** (July 2026). Carriers have pulled back in wildfire areas, and owners shouldn't treat the FAIR Plan as a long-term fix.

### Ventura County context
Foothill and wildland-urban interface areas carry the most risk: Ojai, parts of Ventura's hillsides, Santa Paula, Fillmore, Camarillo/Somis, Thousand Oaks, Simi Valley and Moorpark. The 2017 Thomas Fire and the 2024 Mountain Fire near Camarillo are why buyers ask.

### So what
- **Before listing**, get the current policy, the premium history and a fresh quote. Put the actual number in the OM.
- A buyer's lender will use a real quote. A surprise premium late in escrow can shrink the loan by a large amount and blow up the deal.
- Hardening work, such as defensible space, Class A roofing and ember-resistant vents, can widen the carrier market.
keyPoints: Lenders need replacement-cost coverage from acceptable carriers; FAIR Plan fire-only plus a DIC wrap is a common accepted structure
Insurance comes straight off NOI, so a premium spike shrinks the loan
Example: premium $1,900 to $4,900 cut DSCR from 1.17 to 1.06; some lenders stress premiums +20%
FAIR Plan exposure up 234% to about $700B; residential policies up 151% since Sept 2022 (July 2026)

answers.summary: 2–4 unit buyers use residential financing. In Ventura County the 2026 conforming limits run up to $1,990,450 for a fourplex. Investors need about 25% down for conventional loans, 25% to 30% for DSCR loans, and pay rates in the 6s to 7s. Owner-occupants can put far less down, but must qualify on DTI with only part of the rents counted.
answers.answer:
### Loan limits (Ventura County, 2026 conforming)
| Units | Limit |
|---|---|
| 1 | $1,035,000 |
| 2 | $1,325,000 |
| 3 | $1,601,600 |
| 4 | $1,990,450 |

Loans above these limits are jumbo or portfolio loans.

### Rates (late Oct 2026)
- Freddie Mac's PMMS 30-year fixed averaged **7.32% on Oct. 22, 2026** (7.40% the week before; 6.19% a year earlier). That is the owner-occupied benchmark. Investment properties price higher.
- **DSCR loans** (qualify on the property, not personal income): roughly **6.1%–7.75%** in mid-to-late 2026 lender grids. 2–4 units cost an extra 0.125–0.375 points.

### Down payment and qualifying
| Buyer | Typical down payment | Qualifying |
|---|---|---|
| Owner-occupant, conventional or FHA | low down payment options exist for 2–4 unit primary residences | Personal DTI; lenders count only part of the rents |
| Investor, conventional | **~25% minimum** | Personal DTI and reserves |
| Investor, DSCR loan | **~25%–30%** for 2–4 units | Property DSCR ~1.0x+; 1.20–1.25x prices better; credit floor ~620–680 |

### The math problem
A **$1.6M fourplex**, 25% down, **$1.2M loan at 7.5%** = about **$8,390/month** principal and interest. Add about $1,470/month of property tax at ~1.1%, plus insurance and repairs. Ventura County fourplex rents often don't cover that, so DSCR loans fall short and conventional loans lean on the borrower's income.

### So what
The 2–4 unit market is driven by **owner-users** (house hacking with low down payments), **1031 buyers with big equity**, and **cash buyers**. When pricing a fourplex, figure out which of those buyers you're targeting. A pure investor using a DSCR loan at 7%+ usually can't pay a cap rate in the 4s.

Investor conventional 2–4 units: about 25% down; DSCR loans: 25%–30% down, rates ~6.1%–7.75%
$1.2M at 7.5% over 30 years = about $8,390/month P&I

answers.summary: Seller financing is still a minority tool, but it is used more when rates are high and the seller owns free and clear, which describes many long-time Ventura County owners. It works best on small buildings: the seller earns interest and spreads the gain over time, and the buyer gets financing that banks won't match.
answers.answer:
### Where it shows up
- **Free-and-clear, long-held** small buildings (2–20 units), where the owner wants income more than cash today
- Deals where **DSCR limits the bank loan** (Q108) and the buyer needs a **seller second** to fill the gap. Agency loans generally **don't allow hard subordinate debt**, so seller seconds pair with bank or CU loans, if the lender allows them
- Buildings that are hard to finance: deferred maintenance, fire-zone insurance problems, unpermitted units, or low in-place rents

### Typical structures (negotiated; not standardized)
- Meaningful buyer down payment (often 20%–35%) so the buyer has real money at risk
- Interest-only or 25–30 year amortization with a **5–10 year balloon**
- Rate at or near market, often below the bank rate as a selling point
- Deed of trust with acceleration on sale, insurance and tax impounds, and personal guaranties

### Seller benefits and risks
- **Tax**: an installment sale reports gain **as principal is received**, which spreads the capital gain over several years (Q174). Depreciation recapture taxed as ordinary income doesn't defer. Interest must meet IRS **applicable federal rate (AFR)** minimums.
- **Risk**: if the buyer defaults, the seller may have to foreclose and take back a property in worse shape. Underwrite the buyer like a lender would.

### Frequency
I found **no current data** on seller-carry share in Ventura County. Treat it as uncommon but growing: commercial debt is still expensive versus 2021, and banks remain selective.

### So what
For a free-and-clear owner who doesn't need all the cash, a carryback can **widen the buyer pool and support price**. Bring in the client's CPA and a real estate attorney early. Consumer lending rules can apply if the buyer is an owner-occupant of a 1–4 unit property.
keyPoints: Most common with free-and-clear, long-held small buildings
Installment sale: gain taxed as principal is received; ordinary-income recapture doesn't defer; interest must meet AFR
Agency loans generally prohibit hard subordinate debt, so seller seconds pair with bank or CU loans
Typical structure: 20%–35% down, 5–10 year balloon (negotiated)

answers.summary: Agency loans carry yield maintenance or defeasance by default, with step-downs available for extra cost. Banks and credit unions tend to use step-downs or no penalty at all. The penalty is largest when today's rates are below the loan's note rate, so owners who financed in 2023–2024 at 6.5% to 7% may face six-figure exit costs. Selling with an assumption can avoid that.
answers.answer:
### The structures
| Structure | How it works | Where you see it |
|---|---|---|
| **Yield maintenance (YM)** | Lender is paid the present value of the interest it loses (note rate minus Treasury yield) through the term | Fannie Small default; Freddie before securitization |
| **Defeasance** | Borrower buys Treasuries that replace the loan's cash flows | Freddie Conventional Small after the 2-year lockout; CMBS |
| **Step-down** | Fixed percentage of balance that declines each year, e.g., 5-4-3-2-1 | Agency at extra cost; common at banks |
| **None** | No penalty | Some CUs (e.g., OCCU) |

Freddie Conventional Small: YM until securitized, then a **2-year lockout**, then defeasance, with **no premium in the final 90 days**. Fannie Small offers YM or step-down and is **assumable for a 1% fee** plus costs.

### Why timing matters
YM costs more when rates **fall** below the note rate.
- **2021 loan at ~3.5%** with Treasuries now near 4.8%–5%: the YM formula gives about zero, and the seller usually pays only the minimum premium. That's a cheap exit.
- **2023 loan at 6.75%**, $3M balance, 7 years left, Treasury ~4.9%: rough YM is about 1.85% × $3M a year, discounted over 7 years, or **about $320,000 (~11%)**.

### Seller playbook
- Pull the **note's prepayment rider** before you price a listing. Calculate the exit cost.
- **Time the sale** to a step-down date, the open window (Freddie's last 90 days), or a point where YM has dropped.
- **Market the loan assumption**. A below-market assumable rate is worth real money to buyers, and the 1% fee is cheap compared with YM.
- Research on Fannie small loans shows **prepayments spike when penalties expire**. Expect more listings around those dates.

### So what
Two identical buildings can need very different prices. The difference is often the seller's prepay, so build it into the net-sheet conversation on day one.
keyPoints: Fannie Small: YM or step-down; assumable for a 1% fee
Freddie Conventional Small: YM until securitized, then 2-yr lockout, then defeasance; open the final 90 days
YM grows when market rates fall below the note rate
Example: $3M at 6.75%, 7 years left, Treasury ~4.9%: YM about $320K (~11%)
Prepayments spike when penalty periods expire

answers.summary: A 50 bp move in loan rates changes how much a DSCR-limited buyer can borrow by about 5%, which moves what they can pay by about 3%. On a $5.7M building that is roughly $150K to $170K either way, before any change in cap rates. In practice, cap rates follow rates only partly and with a lag.
answers.answer:
### Worked example (illustrative assumptions)
- NOI **$300,000**, priced at a **5.25% cap** = **$5,714,000**
- Loan: 30-yr amortization, **1.25x** DSCR test, base rate **6.75%** (about where 10-yr agency small debt prices with the 10-yr Treasury near 5%)
- Buyer's equity is fixed at what the base case needs

| Rate | Loan constant | Max loan (NOI ÷ 1.25 ÷ constant) | LTV at base price | Price buyer can pay |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6.25% (−50) | 7.39% | $3,248,000 | 56.8% | **$5,879,000 (+2.9%)** |
| 6.75% (base) | 7.78% | $3,084,000 | 54.0% | $5,714,000 |
| 7.25% (+50) | 8.19% | $2,932,000 | 51.3% | **$5,563,000 (−2.7%)** |

### Cap-rate view
If buyers pass rate changes into cap rates:
- **+25 bps** (5.25% to 5.50%): $300K NOI is worth $5,455,000 (**−4.5%**)
- **−25 bps** (to 5.00%): worth $6,000,000 (**+5.0%**)

Cap rates usually move **less than** the full rate change and more slowly. Nationally, small multifamily cap rates averaged about **6.0% in Q2 2026** with rates near these levels. Spreads have been squeezed and negative leverage is common.

### Reality check for 2026
The 10-year Treasury went from 4.69% (Aug 11) to around 5.1%–5.2% in mid-October, then 4.96% (Oct 22). That is a 30–50 bp swing in a few weeks. Rate locks and timing matter.

### So what
- Tell sellers: **+50 bps ≈ about 3% off what a leveraged buyer can pay**. It's more if cap rates also widen.
- Cash and 1031 buyers with heavy equity are **less rate-sensitive**. They set the price when rates spike.
- Suggest buyers lock early (agency **Index Lock**, rate lock at application) when markets are volatile.
keyPoints: DSCR-limited loan sizing: ±50 bps changes max loan by about ±5%
At fixed equity, that moves the price a buyer can pay by about ±3% (about ±$150–170K on $5.7M)
±25 bps on a 5.25% cap moves value about −4.5% / +5.0%
Cap rates usually follow interest rates only partly and with a lag
10-yr UST swung 4.69% (Aug 11) to ~5.2% (mid-Oct) to 4.96% (Oct 22, 2026)
